chunks.text: Hi, NZCA. Can you give me a thumbs up if you can hear me? Just a mic check. And welcome to the select committee this afternoon, the Environment Select Committee. This is the very first of our hearings for the Conservation Amendment Bill, and we would like to welcome our first submitter, the New Zealand Conservation Authority. Welcome to the committee. We can see you there.

We've got Chad, Dean, and Mick. So look, you've got 15 minutes with us this afternoon, so we'll hand it over to you for some opening remarks and a bit of an introduction. Do take your submission as read, and I'm sure members will have some questions. So if you can leave some time at the end for some questions, that would be great. So over to you.

Madam Chair and members of the committee, tena koutou katoa. Thank you for the opportunity to appear before you today on behalf of the New Zealand Conservation Authority. The Authority acknowledges the work of the committee in considering this bill and the many perspectives you will hear throughout this process. For those unfamiliar with the Authority, we are an independent statutory body established under the Conservation Act, responsible for advising the Minister of Conservation and the Department, approving national conservation planning documents, and reviewing and reporting

on system effectiveness. My name is Shad Rawlinson, Chair of the Authority, and I'm joined by Mick Abbott and Dean van Merlo, both members of the Authority. The Authority supports reform that improves conservation management while retaining conservation primacy, upholding Treaty commitments, preserving independent governance, and maintaining public participation. To make the best use of our time together, we've tried to keep our remarks brief, to allow for those conversations and discussions to occur.

I'll briefly talk about Treaty matters, Mick will pick up on conservation purpose, and Dean will follow on public participation. The Authority supports much of what proposed Section 4A seeks to achieve in the bills. Clearer engagement processes, transparency, and certainty are positive developments.

Our concern is that Section 4A should not unintentionally become the complete code for Treaty compliance. Section 4 of the Conservation Act is one of New Zealand's strongest Treaty provisions. The courts have recognized that it creates substantive obligations capable of influencing outcomes, not simply procedural requirements.

If compliance with Section 4A comes to be treated as satisfying Section 4, the bill narrows and limits those existing obligations. Our recommendation is straightforward: clarify that Section 4A establishes minimum procedural requirements only and does not limit or replace the wider obligation arising under Section 4.

The Authority is also concerned that proposed Section 14ZG removes the only Treaty-based pathway for considering competitive concession processes. We recommend it be amended so that Treaty rights and interests remain a relevant consideration for decision-makers. And a last point in relation to this topic, the Authority doesn't speak for iwi and hapū when it comes to Treaty settlements.

Our role is institutional. We seek to ensure Treaty settlement arrangements operating through the Authority and conservation boards continue to have the same practical and legal effect. Many settlements provide for an enhanced role in conservation decision-making through the Authority and conservation boards. As the statutory framework changes, the bill should ensure those arrangements retain equivalent effect, not simply equivalent consultation processes.

The Authority believes these issues can be addressed through targeted amendments while fully supporting the bill's broader objective of improved conservation management. Madam Chair, I'll pass over to Mick, who will talk about round-off comments around purpose of the bills. Kia ora. The Conservation Authority supports the formulation adopted in the new Section 6E, where it retains the Department's recreation function, and it usefully adds the qualifier to the extent consistent with their conservation.

That correctly establishes conservation as the primary constraint on the Department's functions on public conservation land. Our concern is that the new section, Section 6EA, omits that same qualifier. Rather, the section requires the Department to enable economic use and development to the greatest extent practicable under this Act and other enactments. This is an operational test, and it's rel-- not a conservation test. There is no requirement that economic use and development be consistent with conservation. Three consequences follow.

First, there's no hierarchy between the functions. Section 6EA sits alongside the conservation functions, not beneath them, and can therefore be balanced against them. Second, there's no limitation on scale Significant qualifier. Third, to the greatest extent practical is a maximisation imperative. It removes a consistency constraint. It directs the department towards enabling development irrespective of conservation outcomes.

The practical effect is to redefine conservation as no longer focused on preservation and protection, but on enabling use. Other department to encourage and enable farming, mining, minerals processing, forestry, solar and wind farms, hydroelectric dams, et cetera.

It could also mean new hotels, restaurants, gondolas, and visitor centres in areas of international, national, and regional conservation significance. And because the same function is inserted into Sections 13 , Section 13 governing area plans, and Section 14 governing concessions, it flows through the entire management framework.

We also note that the department's own supplementary analysis report of April 2026 states that conservation will remain the primary purpose of the Conservation Act, and that the changes are intended to enable development.

None of this has been translated into the drafting. The NZCA recommends that the Section 6 be removed, or if it is to remain, it should be amended to read, "To recognise the economic opportunities that arise from the use and development of land and other natural resources and historic resources managed by the department, and to allow their use conservation."

That single change would apply to tourism, to visitor amenity areas, and to all other economic use and development. It would require development proposals to demonstrate how conservation benefit accrues from their implementation. I'll now pass on to Dean van Melsem to discuss public participation in terms of the bill.

Good afternoon, Madam Chair, members of the committee. Improved and more efficient conservation planning processes and greater certainty and faster turnaround in concession processing are both legitimate objectives of the Conservation Amendment Bill that the NZCA supports. There's no doubt that the conservation planning system can and should be improved and made more efficient.

Such improvement, however, does not require dismantling the independent oversight that has underpinned the management of New Zealand's conservation lands and waters for almost four decades. Conservation boards throughout the country and the NZCA at a national level provide independent community-based input and conservation governance.

Concentrating national policy, regional planning, and concession authority in a single ministerial office, while simultaneously mandating an economic development function for all public conservation lands and waters, fundamentally rewrites the architecture of the Conservation Act and those acts listed in its first schedule.

Rather than modernising conservation law, the Conservation Amendment Bill returns us to the early 1980s, where multiple conflicting conservation and development or use imperatives were simultaneously sought to be given effect to by government departments. Under the bill, the minister will set the NCPS, approve all area plans under it, and make concession decisions, while at the same time enabling economic development to the greatest extent practicable.

It is to address these sorts of conflicts that the Conservation Act separates rule setting and rule application. Conservation boards and the NZCA have an important role in policy and rule setting. That role is a conduit for community engagement. Remove the role, and we risk losing that engagement and community buy-in to the protection and management of our nation's conservation resources.

Outcomes for conservation are known to be more effective and more enduring where the community is engaged and listened to. The NZCA recommends that its oversight role as a decision-maker is retained in the development of the National Conservation Policy Statement, and that conservation boards, is retained in respect of conservation area plans under the Amendment Bill.

The authority considers that watering down the authority and the board's planning functions to an advisory role only would be retrograde and counter to progressive and modern conservation management, which encourages community input and engagement. We envisage an optimal solution where the NCPS is jointly approved by the minister and the NZCA, and subsidiary area plans are approved by conservation boards consistent with their place-based knowledge and statutory mandate.

The NZCA supports the retention of targeted public hearings for both plan-making and concession decision processes. From a practical perspective, our experience is that hearings convened under the existing provisions of the Conservation Act are very efficiently managed and do not suffer the lengthy processes that have become commonplace in some other forums.

Finally, the NZCA acknowledges that within its memberships, and within the membership of many conservation boards, there are placements that are the result of finalized treaty settlements. The authority is concerned that removing or reducing the statutory role of boards and the authority risks undermining these existing settlements. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Look, we have about five minutes for questions, so we will start with Priyanka. Thank you. And firstly, I just want to say thank you. That was an exceptional submission, I thought. You laid out your rationale really clearly, so thank you for that I have to choose between two questions now that I have for you.

But I think I'll ask you, in your written submission in 5.4, I think it is, you have suggested that the committee seeks specific evidence of NZCA or board-caused material delay before the efficiency rationale is removed, to ostensibly speed up the process.

Can I ask whether DOC has ever communicated to the Conservation Authority that there have been delays caused by the authority? In my assessment, no. We have a statutory role when it comes to approving plans, and we're pretty much toward the end of the process.

Boards develop plans along with local DOC, the local DOC regional area, and those are developed in partnership with where there are treaty settlement arrangements. And then they get passed through particular decision-making gateways before it ultimately lands in front of the authority.

I've been on the authority three years, and we've just approved the Te Hiku CMS at our last meeting. And I understand that was in about a three-year development process. We had to pause the West Coast CMS because of the reform program. That was in development. And the last plan that was approved, and it was an update to an existing plan, I think was in 2022, I think. I'll just check with Dean and Mick on those two matters.

Yeah. Thank you. If the issue is indeed time frames and delays, and there was perhaps a specific time frame written into this legislation, would you be supportive of that? And what do you think a reasonable time frame for response from NZCA would be? I might pass to Dean or to Mick, who might have comments on that.

You can also come back to us. Yeah, I think it's perfectly good to streamline and to set a time frame for those things. In terms of conservation boards, it depends on the facilitation that the department can give to that process and also working with iwi partners. For the authority's role in that with the current CMSs that we've done, I would imagine a six month is sufficient time frame for doing things.

Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Celia Wade-Brown. Thank you very much. Thank you for a comprehensive submission. I've got a couple of questions. You've got one. You're shuffling around. I've got more than a couple, but I will ask one. Yes. Which is, the debate about the changes to the Conservation Act are very much framed as economic versus conservation.

And do you think from your experience, seeing people coming through using the conservation estate, that the benefits to mental and physical health for people actually getting out and about have been almost ignored in that fight between conservation and more extractive economic benefit?

I might pass to Dean. He might be able to share some comments on that one. Well, my response to that would be undoubtedly those benefits are there, and they are huge. They are rather intangible, so of course, they're rather difficult to quantify. Some people have attempted to and even tried to apply an economic analysis to that.

But I think it's generally accepted that there are huge benefits to the population at large, to people getting out and enjoying the public conservation land. And, I know DOC has made a real push for promoting that in recent years, and I think that's a real positive step that we've seen.

Thank you. I don't know if I can take it further than that. Thank you. Grant McCallum. Yeah, just focusing on the governance and your role in this space. Given that the minister is the one ultimately responsible to the public and for the outcomes of the plans and so forth, shouldn't the minister therefore have the final say?

I think reflecting on history and why the NZCA and the authorities were put in place, it was to manage the tension between, at the time, pre-DOC, you've got liens and survey, you've got forestry department looking after assets, and there was this inherent tension between economic development and preservation.

And I suppose the way the bills are framed, we could potentially be heading back into that inherent tension within conservation around how we manage our important spaces and resources. At the same time, the tension and the push for development. So the role of the authority was to create that separation, along with the conservation boards, but also to provide for public voice in these processes.

Yeah, but ultimately, they can still do that, but give the minister the final say, since ultimately the minister is the one who has to go out and show the public. Because they're the ones that are directly responsible to the public in the end. Yes. Yeah, and I appreciate that. I think this gives that level of separation and particularly that political dynamic that occurs. The Conservation Authority has a stewardship role in terms of holding a space for all New Zealanders, regardless of the political environment that New

Zealand sits in. I'd add just in that, the conservation boards represent the public in their public conservation lands, but the board members and the authority members are actually appointed by the Minister of Conservation. Thank you. Look, I'm just going to quickly jump in because I'm quite interested in the recommendation around 6E .

And obviously you have said that you'd like to see it removed, otherwise, amended, so that economic development activities must be consistent with conservation. Did you have any kind of wording or any kind of further thoughts around tying those together?

We've suggested at the end there some specific wording for that. And in terms of that consistent with conservation, we feel that makes available many opportunities within tourism and other areas, but making sure that conservation is prioritized and benefits from any such activities.

Okay. Thank you. And we'll just take one last quick question from Scott. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you all. It's related to those other two questions. Essentially, the point that you make about the lack of hierarchy in 6E is something that we can see the risk with that. And I really just want to get your sense of what do you think could be the effect of this for our tourism dollar, for people who come to Aotearoa for the clean green image, for the unique experiences they can have in our wilderness.

What do you think could be the effect if we don't have that conservation value at top of the hierarchy? Pass to Dean or to Mick. I'll just add in there, I think that having that consistent with conservation, I think would provide wonderful focus for tourism and other interests to- Mm to continue that development and promotion of tourism. That is actually why people are coming here.

So we don't see that as a conflict rather than an alignment. That's great. Look- Yeah. I'd concur with that, and I'd just briefly add that I think there is great reputational risk to New Zealand's hard-earned reputation. We've marketed ourselves on 100% pure, et cetera. And potentially if we undermine that, I think the consequences could be quite significant.

Look, thank you very much. We are going to have to leave it there. We've met time. We really appreciate your submission, a really valuable submission with a lot to think about there. So, thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. So that brings us to the end of our public hearings on the Conservation Amendment Bill
